title: Unauthenticated pol_round in arc-node: From Hash Preimage Omission to State Divergence
summary_en: An omission of the pol_round field from the proposal hash lets an attacker change the round value without breaking the proposer’s Ed25519 signature, causing divergent voting and possible consensus stall.

lesson.cause: The root cause is three‑fold. First, the ProposalParts::hash function builds a Keccak‑256 hash using only height, round, and data bytes, completely leaving out the pol_round field. Second, the validate_proposal_parts routine verifies the proposer’s Ed25519 signature against this incomplete hash, so any change to pol_round does not affect signature validity. Third, the assemble_block_from_parts function copies the attacker‑controlled pol_round directly into the block’s valid_round state, allowing the manipulated value to influence the consensus state machine.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher opened the source file crates/types/src/proposal_parts.rs to see how the proposal hash is built.
hasher.update(self.height().as_u64().to_be_bytes());
hasher.update(self.round().as_i64().to_be_bytes());
for data in &self.data { hasher.update(&data.bytes); }
Why: hash means a fixed‑size digest; Keccak‑256 is the hash algorithm. The code shows only height, round, and data are fed, so pol_round is never included.

DISCOVERY
Step 2: The researcher inspected the signature check in crates/malachite-app/src/proposal_parts.rs.
hash = parts.hash()
Why: validate_proposal_parts fetches the hash computed in Step 1 and then verifies the Ed25519 signature against it. Because the hash lacks pol_round, the signature does not bind that field.

STEP 3: The researcher read the block assembly code in state_machine.rs (line 279).
valid_round: parts.init().pol_round
Why: assemble_block_from_parts writes the pol_round value from the proposal directly into the node’s consensus state, so a modified value becomes the official round.

EXPLOITATION
Step 4: The researcher wrote a Python PoC to compute the hash and sign it, then altered pol_round from 0 to 5 and re‑used the same signature.
def proposal_parts_hash(height_u64, round_i64, data_parts):
    msg = bytearray()
    msg.extend(height_u64.to_bytes(8, 'big'))
    msg.extend(round_i64.to_bytes(8, 'big', signed=True))
    for part in data_parts:
        msg.extend(part)
    return keccak_256(bytes(msg))
Why: Python code builds the exact byte sequence used by the Rust hash function, proving that the hash does not depend on pol_round.

Step 5: The PoC printed the verification result.
BEFORE pol_round=0, AFTER pol_round=5, SIGNATURE VALID: True
Why: The signature remains valid after changing pol_round, confirming the omission bug.

IMPACT
Step 6: The researcher explained how the altered valid_round affects the voting guard in prevote_previous.
vr = proposal.pol_round()
if locked.round <= vr: prevote Val(proposed) else: prevote Nil
Why: prevote is a vote for the next block; Val means a positive vote, Nil means abstain. Different nodes receiving different pol_round values will take different branches, leading to conflicting votes and possible consensus split or stall.

STEP 7: The researcher noted that no private key is needed—only network access to relay tampered proposals.
Why: Because the signature verification does not cover pol_round, an attacker can simply forward modified messages without possessing any validator key.
lesson.takeaway: When reviewing consensus or blockchain code, always check that every mutable field influencing state transitions is included in the signed hash. Look for hash construction functions that skip fields like round, epoch, or timestamps. Tools such as grep for "hash.update" or static analysis can highlight missing inputs. Variants of this bug appear in other protocols that sign only a subset of a message (e.g., missing chain‑id in Ethereum signatures). Beginners often assume a signature automatically protects the whole object and forget to verify the exact signed data.

title: Server-Side reCAPTCHA Validation Bypass on /services/request-send.php
summary_en: The POST endpoint /services/request-send.php accepts form data without verifying the reCAPTCHA token on the server, so an attacker can send an empty g-recaptcha-response and still create leads.

lesson.cause: reCAPTCHA (a challenge‑response test that proves a user is human) is presented in the web form and generates a token stored in the g-recaptcha-response parameter (a field sent in the HTTP request body). The server‑side script request‑send.php (code that runs on the web server) does not verify that this parameter is present or valid before processing the request. It only records the CAPTCHA validation result in the JSON response but does not abort the workflow (the sequence of actions such as lead creation and email notification) when the result is false. Because the check occurs after lead creation, missing or invalid tokens are ignored, allowing unauthenticated users to bypass the protection.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Open the form in a browser (a program that displays web pages). Why: to see the fields and the reCAPTCHA widget (a visual challenge that generates a token).
Step 2: Capture the network traffic with Burp Suite (a proxy tool that lets you view and modify HTTP requests). Why: to see the exact request the browser sends.
DISCOVERY
Step 3: Locate the g-recaptcha-response parameter in the captured request. Why: this parameter carries the token that the server expects.
Step 4: Send the captured request to Burp Repeater (a feature that lets you resend and edit a request). Why: to experiment with modifications.
EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Edit the request body to set g-recaptcha-response= (empty). The exact request:
POST /services/request-send.php HTTP/2
Host: birdviewpsa.com

title: When Deleting the Default Workspace Made the Entire Account Unusable
summary_en: An attacker could delete a 'protected' default workspace by manually changing the workspace ID in a deletion request, causing the entire account to become unusable.

lesson.cause: The application relied on frontend restrictions—simply hiding a button—to protect the default workspace instead of enforcing the rule on the server. The backend endpoint '/customer-service/workspace/v1/delete-workspace/{workspace_id}' accepted any valid workspace ID without verifying if that specific ID was marked as 'non-deletable' or 'system-required.' This allowed a user to bypass the user interface (UI) and trigger a deletion that the system's logic was not designed to handle, leading to a crash.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher logged into the application and identified a 'Default Workspace' that is automatically created for every user.
2. They observed that while other workspaces had a 'Delete' button in the UI (User Interface: the visual part of the app you click on), the Default Workspace did not.
DISCOVERY
3. To understand how the application handles deletions, the researcher created a temporary workspace named 'test'.
4. They opened a proxy tool (software that lets you see and change messages between your browser and the server) to capture the HTTP request (a message sent from your browser to a server to perform an action).
5. They clicked 'Delete' on the 'test' workspace and captured the following request:
GET /customer-service/workspace/v1/delete-workspace/12345
(Why: This reveals the endpoint (a specific web address for a task) and the workspace ID (a unique number identifying a specific folder)).
EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher needed the ID for the 'Default Workspace'. They found it by inspecting the page's HTML (the underlying code used to structure a webpage).
7. They assumed the Default Workspace ID was '999'.
8. Using the proxy tool, they manually crafted a new request, replacing the 'test' ID with the 'Default' ID.
GET /customer-service/workspace/v1/delete-workspace/999
(Why: This tests if the backend (the server's brain) checks if the ID is allowed to be deleted, or if it just follows any command it receives).
9. The researcher sent the modified request to the server.
10. The server responded with a '200 OK' status (a standard response code meaning the server successfully processed the request).
IMPACT
11. The researcher refreshed the application to see the results.
12. The 'Default Workspace' was gone, but the application now displayed a completely blank page.
13. They attempted to log out and log back in, but the application became stuck on a 'loading' screen.
14. This confirmed a Denial of Service (a state where a user is prevented from using the application) because the system's business logic (the rules of how the app works) required the Default Workspace to exist to function.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional cloud storage site 'target.example'. When you sign up, you get a 'Primary Folder' that cannot be deleted in the settings menu. However, the site uses a link like 'https://target.example/api/remove?folder_id=101' to delete folders. If a user manually types 'https://target.example/api/remove?folder_id=PRIMARY_ID' into their browser, the server deletes it because it doesn't check if the ID belongs to the protected Primary Folder. Since the website's code is programmed to always open the Primary Folder upon login, the site now crashes for that user because it cannot find the folder it needs to start.
lesson.takeaway: Always test actions that are 'hidden' or 'disabled' in the UI by capturing a valid request for a similar allowed action and swapping the ID. This is a form of IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference), where you manipulate an ID to perform unauthorized actions. Look for 'Default', 'System', or 'Admin' objects that the application might depend on to function, as deleting them often causes high-impact business logic failures. A common mistake is assuming that if a button is missing, the server is automatically safe.

title: When a Production Backend Has No Authentication: Internal Disclosure and Unauthenticated State…
summary_en: A Spring Boot commerce backend exposed its OpenAPI spec and all business endpoints without any authentication, allowing anyone to read internal details and submit orders anonymously.

lesson.cause: The root cause was the complete absence of an authentication layer. The OpenAPI document (/v3/api-docs) did not define any security scheme, so the server advertised no auth requirement. Each business operation, including the order‑submission endpoint, also lacked code that checks for a valid session, token, or API key. Because the developers relied on the OpenAPI spec to convey security, they never added runtime checks. Consequently, the service treated every HTTP request as trusted, exposing both data and state‑changing actions to the public internet.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the target host and base path.
GET https://example.com/v3/api-docs
Why: Sends an HTTP GET request (a request to retrieve data) to the OpenAPI endpoint; the response code 200 shows the service is reachable without credentials.
Step 2: Examine the returned OpenAPI JSON for a "security" field.
Why: The OpenAPI spec defines authentication requirements; the absence of a "security" object confirms no auth is required (no "Authorization" header needed).
DISCOVERY
Step 3: List all paths from the OpenAPI document.
Why: The spec lists every endpoint (e.g., /order, /metrics); this gives a map of the application without guessing URLs.
Step 4: Locate a state‑changing endpoint such as the order‑submission path.
Why: Business operations are described in the spec; finding a POST method indicates a write operation.
EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Craft an HTTP POST request to the order endpoint with a JSON body you control.
POST https://example.com/order
Content-Type: application/json
{ "product_id": "123", "quantity": 1 }
Why: Sends a payload (data sent to the server) that the endpoint accepts; no Authorization header is needed, so the request is accepted anonymously.
Step 6: Observe the HTTP 200 response with an acknowledgement message.
Why: The server returns a success code, proving the operation succeeded without authentication.
IMPACT
Step 7: Note that internal diagnostics (e.g., /actuator/info, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/peer-info) also return data without auth.
Why: These endpoints expose build metadata, internal IPs, and service dependencies, giving an attacker a detailed view of the environment.
lesson.example:
**Fictional vulnerable service**: https://target.example/api
- Vulnerable endpoint: POST /api/create‑order
- Expected auth: Bearer token in Authorization header (but missing).
- Attack request:
POST https://target.example/api/create-order
Content-Type: application/json
{ "item":"widget", "qty":5 }
Why it works: The server does not check for an Authorization header, so the JSON payload is processed as a legitimate order. The response contains "order received" confirming the state change.
lesson.takeaway: When an API publishes its OpenAPI/Swagger spec publicly, always verify the "security" section; a missing scheme often means the endpoints are unauthenticated. Look for unauthenticated access to /actuator/*, /metrics, or any POST/PUT routes. Tools like `curl`, `httpie`, or Burp Suite can quickly fetch the spec and test endpoints. Variants include services that rely on network‑level firewalls instead of auth, or that expose admin consoles without login. Beginners often forget to test POST endpoints after seeing a public spec, assuming they are protected; always try them.
lesson.fix: Add a global authentication requirement in the Spring Boot configuration (e.g., `spring.security.enabled=true`). Define a security scheme in the OpenAPI spec and enforce it at runtime with Spring Security filters that reject requests lacking a valid token or session cookie. Restrict actuator endpoints to internal IPs or require authentication (`management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info` only). Remove or protect build‑metadata endpoints (`/actuator/info`) and ensure they are not exposed publicly. Finally, verify the OpenAPI document reflects the actual security controls to avoid mismatches.

summary_en: A negative quantity can be submitted to the checkout API, causing the cart total to become negative and granting the attacker a monetary credit. The flaw stems from missing server‑side validation of numeric inputs.

title: How a Simple Negative Quantity Exposed a Serious Checkout Logic Flaw
summary_en: A negative quantity value in the checkout request bypasses validation, creates a negative subtotal and forces the payable amount to zero while keeping the cart active, enabling free purchases.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a missing server‑side validation rule for the *quantity* field. The backend accepts any integer, including negative numbers, and stores it in the cart. Because the pricing engine blindly multiplies *unit price* by *quantity*, a negative quantity produces a negative subtotal. The application then fails to reject a negative subtotal and sets *total_payable* to 0.0, leaving the cart in a normal *CART* state. Additionally, the checkout operation relied on a public session identifier without an authorization header, allowing the manipulated cart to be used without proper ownership checks.

Step 1: Capture a normal checkout request.

Why: This is the typical *HTTP request* body sent to the *endpoint* that processes the cart; it shows the expected *parameter* structure.

Step 2: Identify the *quantity* parameter inside the JSON.
Why: *Parameter* is a named value the server reads; here it controls how many units are bought.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: Modify the *quantity* to a negative number.

{ "items": [ { "quantity": -1 } ] }
Why: Sending *-1* tests how the server handles unexpected numeric input; *-* is the minus sign indicating a negative integer.

Step 5: Reload the checkout page (a new *HTTP GET* to the cart endpoint) using the same session.
Why: To verify persistence; the server should retrieve the stored cart data.

Step 6: Observe that the cart still shows the negative quantity and a “FREE!” total.
Why: The malicious value was saved in the database, so subsequent reads return the corrupted state.

IMPACT
Step 7: Note that the cart remains in the *CART* state, not an error state.
Why: The application does not perform a final validation before allowing the order to proceed, so the attacker could potentially complete the purchase at zero cost.

A common beginner mistake is to assume the front‑end validation is sufficient; always verify the back‑end enforces business rules.

summary_en: A business logic flaw allowed users to manipulate the price of services during checkout by tampering with the 'amount' parameter in the HTTP request, enabling the purchase of expensive hosting for negligible sums.

lesson.cause: The application's backend trusted the client-side browser to provide the correct price for a transaction. Specifically, the /gateway/process endpoint accepted an 'amount' parameter directly from the user's POST request (a message sent to the server to submit data). Instead of the server looking up the verified price in its own database using the 'invoiceid', it blindly accepted whatever number the user provided and passed it to the payment gateway.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher selected a hosting service and generated an invoice on the platform.
2. They navigated to the checkout view at the endpoint (a specific web address) /viewinvoice.php.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher opened Burp Suite (a tool used to intercept and modify web traffic) to monitor the communication between their browser and the server.
4. They clicked the payment button and intercepted the outgoing POST request (a type of HTTP request used to send data to a server).
5. They inspected the request body to identify how the price was being sent.
POST /gateway/process HTTP/2
Host: redacted.example.com
invoiceid=REDACTED&amount=4606800000&email=user%40example.com&pay=Submit
Why: This revealed that the 'amount' (the price) was being sent as a parameter (a piece of data) that could be easily edited by the user.
EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher sent the intercepted request to the Burp Suite Repeater tool to modify it.
7. They changed the 'amount' value from 4606800000 to a much smaller number.
amount=50000
Why: This tests if the backend (the server-side code) validates the price against the database or trusts the user's input.
8. They forwarded the modified request to the server.
9. The server responded with a 302 Found (a redirect instruction telling the browser to go to a new page).
HTTP/2 302 Found
Location: https://paymentgateway.example.com/payment/token_id
Why: The server accepted the fake price and generated a valid session with the third-party payment provider.
IMPACT
10. The researcher followed the redirect in their browser to the payment gateway.
11. They observed that the payment gateway was now asking for only 50,000 IRR instead of the original price.
Why: This confirms that an attacker could pay a fraction of the cost to receive full services.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site target.example that sells digital gift cards. When you click 'Buy', your browser sends this request: POST /buy-card HTTP/1.1 Host: target.example card_type=gold&price=100.00. A beginner attacker uses a proxy tool to catch this message before it leaves their computer. They change 'price=100.00' to 'price=0.01' and click send. Because the server at target.example just takes that 'price' value and sends it to PayPal, the attacker gets a $100 gift card for one cent. The server should have only asked for the 'card_type' and looked up the price itself in its secure database.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for financial values (price, discount, quantity) being passed in HTTP requests during checkout or cart updates. Use a proxy tool like Burp Suite to see if changing these values results in a lower total at the final payment step. A common signal is seeing both an ID (like invoice_id) and a value (like price) in the same request; the server should only need the ID. A variant of this is 'negative quantities,' where adding -1 of an item might reduce the total price of other items in the cart. Avoid the mistake of assuming that because a field is 'hidden' in the HTML, it cannot be changed by the user.
lesson.fix:
The server must never trust the price sent from the client. The payment initiation endpoint should only accept an invoice identifier. The backend should then fetch the correct amount from the database and send that verified amount to the payment gateway. Additionally, when the payment is finished, the server must verify the 'callback' (the confirmation message from the payment provider) to ensure the amount actually paid matches the amount owed.

title: Broken Access Control: Unauthenticated Read/Write Access to Every Conversation in an Tiktok AI…
summary_en: Multiple endpoints in the TikTok AI chatbot failed to enforce authentication, allowing anyone to list recent conversation IDs and read or send messages to any user's chat history without a login.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a complete failure to implement authentication checks on several backend API endpoints. While the application appeared to check for data ownership when a user provided a session cookie (a small file used to remember your login), it completely skipped all security checks if the cookie was missing entirely. This 'fail-open' logic meant that the server assumed any request without a login was safe to process, likely because developers assumed the conversation IDs (unique identification strings) were secret enough to prevent guessing. Additionally, the existence of a global '/conversations' endpoint that listed the 20 most recent chat IDs without any user-specific filtering allowed for easy discovery of other people's private data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Open the chatbot interface and use a proxy tool to capture the HTTP requests (messages sent from your browser to the server).
2. Identify the endpoint used to create a new chat session.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/create HTTP/1.1
Why: This request initializes a new chat and generates a unique ID for the conversation (a unique identification string).
3. Identify the endpoint used to send a message to the AI.
POST /.../agent/coze/chat HTTP/1.1
Why: This sends the user's text to the chatbot backend.
4. Identify the endpoint used to retrieve the chat history.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1
Why: This loads previous messages so the user can see their conversation history.
DISCOVERY
5. Attempt an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference - a bug where you access data by changing an ID) by keeping your login cookie but changing the 'conversation_id' to one you don't own.
{ "conversation_id": "<foreign_id>" }
Why: To see if the server checks if the logged-in user actually owns that specific chat.
6. Observe that the server returns an empty list, which initially suggests that security checks are in place.
EXPLOITATION
7. Perform a 'no-auth' test by removing the Cookie header (the part of the request that proves you are logged in) and resending the history request.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1 (No Cookie Header)
Why: To check if the server requires a login at all (Authentication: the process of verifying who a user is).
8. Observe that the server returns the full chat history, proving that authentication is not enforced.
9. Search for more sensitive endpoints by guessing variations of the URL, such as changing '/conversation/create' to '/conversations'.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversations HTTP/1.1
Why: Pluralized endpoints often list multiple items; the researcher hoped to find a list of all chats.
10. Observe the response containing a list of the 20 most recent conversation IDs from other users globally.
11. Copy a 'conversation_id' belonging to a different user from that list.
IMPACT
12. Send a message to that foreign ID without being logged in.
POST /.../agent/coze/chat HTTP/1.1 with { "conversation_id": "<stolen_id>", "content": "hi" }
Why: To prove that an attacker can write data (Integrity: the assurance that data is not altered by unauthorized people) to any chat.
13. Request the message history for that same foreign ID.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1 with { "conversation_id": "<stolen_id>" }
Why: To prove that an attacker can read data (Confidentiality: keeping data secret from unauthorized people) from any chat.
14. Confirm the response contains the injected message and the AI's reply, verifying full unauthorized access.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'support-bot.target.example' that lets users chat with a help agent. When you chat, your browser sends a request to 'https://support-bot.target.example/api/get_history?chat_id=99'. Normally, your browser also sends a header like 'Authorization: Bearer xyz123' to prove it is you. An attacker notices this and tries to change the ID to 'chat_id=100' while keeping their token, but the server says 'Access Denied'. However, when the attacker uses a tool to send the request 'GET /api/get_history?chat_id=100' with NO Authorization header at all, the server mistakenly thinks it is a public request and returns the full private chat history of user 100. This happens because the code only checks 'Does this token own this ID?' but forgets to check 'Is there even a token present?' before showing the data.
lesson.takeaway: The most important lesson is to always test endpoints by completely removing authentication headers, not just by swapping user accounts. Developers sometimes implement complex logic to check if 'User A' owns 'Object B', but forget to apply a global 'Is the user logged in?' check (Middleware: code that runs before the main logic to verify security). Look for pluralized endpoints (like /users instead of /user) or administrative-sounding paths, as these are often overlooked during security reviews. A common mistake is assuming that 'unguessable' IDs like long strings of random characters are a substitute for real authentication; they are not.
lesson.fix: The developers must implement a mandatory authentication middleware that runs for every request to the '/agent/' and '/conversation/' paths. This middleware should verify that a valid session exists before any other logic is executed; if no session is found, the request must be rejected with a '401 Unauthorized' error. Furthermore, the database query for retrieving messages should always include a filter for the 'user_id' derived from the authenticated session, like 'SELECT * FROM messages WHERE conversation_id = ? AND owner_id = ?'. This ensures that even if a user is logged in, they can only see conversations that belong to their specific account ID. Finally, the global '/conversations' list endpoint should be restricted to administrative users or removed entirely if not needed for the application's functionality.

title: How a Flawed OTP Flow Led to Full Account Takeover
summary_en: A flawed OTP flow let an attacker generate unlimited valid one‑time passwords and brute‑force them, resulting in full account takeover.

lesson.cause: The platform only attached a cooldown timer to the “Resend OTP” button on the verification page, not to the initial email submission. By navigating back and resubmitting the email, the backend generated a new OTP without any rate‑limit check (cooldown bypass). The server never invalidated previously issued OTPs, so each new code co‑existed with all older ones (state‑management failure). Each OTP remained valid for ten minutes, giving an attacker a large pool of active codes (long TTL). Together these design flaws broke the intended security model of the OTP system.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Enter the victim’s email address on the login page to start the passwordless flow.

Why: This sends an HTTP request that tells the server to generate a 6‑digit OTP for that email.
Step 2: Observe that the server redirects to a verification page that contains a “Resend OTP” button.

Why: The verification page is where the user would normally type the received code.
EXPLOITATION
Step 3: Click the browser’s Back button to return to the original email‑entry page.

Why: Going back bypasses the front‑end cooldown that only protects the “Resend OTP” button.
Step 4: Resubmit the same email address repeatedly, as fast as possible.

Why: Each submission triggers the backend to generate a fresh OTP instantly, because the server does not enforce a rate limit on this endpoint.
Step 5: Note that previously generated OTPs remain valid; the system does not invalidate older codes.

Why: This is the missing OTP invalidation flaw, so all generated codes stay active simultaneously.
Step 6: Open Burp Suite’s Intruder and configure it to send OTP verification requests with random 6‑digit codes.

Why: The attacker now has a large pool of valid codes, so guessing any one of them will succeed.
Step 7: Rotate IP addresses (switch Wi‑Fi, use a mobile hotspot, or a proxy pool) when the firewall returns a 502 Bad Gateway for too many wrong guesses.

Why: The firewall blocks a single IP after many failures; changing IPs avoids the block.
Step 8: Continue brute‑forcing until the server accepts a code and returns an authenticated session cookie.

Why: Once a valid OTP is submitted, the server creates a session, granting full account access.
lesson.example:
Target: target.example offers passwordless login via email OTP.
Vulnerable endpoint: POST https://target.example/api/auth/request-otp with JSON {"email":"user@target.example"}.
The server creates a 6‑digit code, stores it, and returns 200, but does not limit how often the endpoint can be called and does not invalidate previous codes.
An attacker can call the endpoint 5,000 times, obtaining 5,000 active codes that stay valid for 10 minutes.
Then they brute‑force the verification endpoint POST https://target.example/api/auth/verify-otp with {"email":"user@target.example","code":"123456"} until a match is found, gaining full account access.
lesson.takeaway: Hunters should look for OTP endpoints that allow repeated email submissions without server‑side cooldown or OTP invalidation. Test the “Back” button or send direct POST requests to the email‑submission endpoint to see if new codes are issued each time. Verify that generating a new OTP revokes previous ones and that the validity window is short (e.g., 2‑5 minutes). Similar issues appear in password‑reset flows and magic‑link login systems. A common mistake is assuming the front‑end cooldown is enforced server‑side; always test the server directly.

title: Predictable Account-Activation Token: Email-Ownership Verification Bypass
summary_en: An attacker can bypass email verification by calculating the account activation token offline using a simple SHA-1 hash of the user's email address. This allows for full account activation and session hijacking without requiring access to the victim's email inbox.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a deterministic token generation design where the 'secret' activation token was merely a SHA-1 hash of the user's lowercase email address. Because the email address is public knowledge, the token contains zero entropy (unpredictability), allowing anyone to recreate it. Furthermore, the registration API endpoint leaked the 'membershipGuid' (a unique identifier) in its response, providing the attacker with all necessary components to build a valid activation request. The application failed to include a server-side secret or random salt in the hashing process.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher initiates a registration request to the public API.
POST /api/account/register
Why: To observe how the system handles new accounts and what data it returns. (An HTTP request is a message sent from your computer to a server asking for an action).
Step 2: The researcher analyzes the JSON response from the server.
{"resultCode": 1, "membershipGuid": "<membership-guid>", "accessToken": null}
Why: The response provides the 'membershipGuid' needed for later steps and confirms the account is inactive because 'accessToken' is null. (JSON is a text format used to organize and send data).
DISCOVERY
Step 3: The researcher identifies the activation parameters required by the app.
mid = membership identifier, act = activation token
Why: These two pieces of data are the 'keys' needed to unlock the account. (A parameter is a specific piece of information sent to a web address).
Step 4: The researcher collects multiple tokens from different test accounts to find a pattern.
[Token A, Token B, Token C]
Why: Comparing multiple results helps identify if the tokens are random or follow a formula. (A token is a unique string of characters used for security).
Step 5: The researcher tests if the token is a hash of the email.
SHA1(lowercase("test@example.com"))
Why: SHA-1 is a common mathematical formula that turns text into a 40-character code; researchers often check if developers used it lazily. (SHA-1 is a hashing function that creates a unique digital fingerprint of data).
EXPLOITATION
Step 6: The researcher calculates the SHA-1 hash for a target email address offline.
SHA1("victim@example.com") -> 40-character hex string
Why: This creates the 'secret' activation code without ever seeing the actual email sent by the server. (Offline calculation means doing work on your own computer instead of asking the server).
Step 7: The researcher tests an intentionally incorrect token first.
/activate?mid=123&act=wrong_token
Why: To confirm the server actually checks the token and doesn't just activate every account. (Validation is the process of a server checking if data is correct).
Step 8: The researcher submits the final exploit request using the calculated hash.
GET /api/account/activate?mid=<membership-guid>&act=<calculated-sha1>
Why: This sends the guessed 'secret' to the server to prove 'ownership' of the email. (A GET request is a way to ask a server for a specific page or action via a URL).
IMPACT
Step 9: The server accepts the token and redirects to the success flow.
HTTP 302 Redirect
Why: The server was tricked into thinking the researcher clicked the link in the real email. (A redirect tells your browser to go to a different web page automatically).
Step 10: The researcher checks the new cookies issued by the server.
access_token=<new-session-token>
Why: The server now treats the researcher as a logged-in user. (A cookie is a small piece of data a server gives you to remember who you are).
Step 11: The researcher decodes the new access token to verify identity.
{"sub": "user_id_123", "role": "user"}
Why: To prove that the bypass resulted in a real, functioning user session. (An access token is a digital key that grants you entry to protected parts of a site).
Step 12: The researcher confirms the email is now marked as 'verified' in the system.
Email Status: Verified
Why: This completes the bypass, showing that the security check was successfully defeated. (Verification is the proof that a user actually owns the email address they provided).
lesson.example: We assume a fictional site 'target.example' uses MD5 hashes of usernames for password reset links. (MD5 is an older, faster hashing formula). If a user 'admin' forgets their password, the site sends a link like: target.example/reset?user=admin&token=21232f297a57a5a743894a0e4a801fc3. An attacker knows the username is 'admin'. They calculate MD5('admin') which equals '21232f297a57a5a743894a0e4a801fc3'. The attacker then visits that URL directly. Because the token is just a hash of the name, the server accepts it, allowing the attacker to set a new password for the admin account without ever seeing the reset email.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for verification bypasses, always collect 3-5 tokens and check them against common hashing algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) using the email, username, or timestamp as inputs. Use tools like 'Hash Identifier' or online 'CrackStation' to see if the token looks like a known hash format. A major signal is if the token length is always exactly 32, 40, or 64 characters. A common variant is 'Time-Based Tokens' where the token is a hash of the minute the request was made. Avoid the mistake of assuming a long string of characters is 'random' just because it looks complex; if you can recreate it, it isn't random.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, the application must use a Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator (CSPRNG) to create tokens that are impossible to guess. Instead of hashing the email, generate a long, random string (at least 32 characters) and store it in the database linked to the user's account. When the user clicks the link, compare the provided token to the one stored in the database. Example fix in Python: 
import secrets
token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
# Store 'token' in DB associated with the user
# Send 'token' in the email link

title: The Removed Email That Led to a $500 Account Takeover
summary_en: A removed email address could still receive password‑reset links, allowing an attacker who still controls that email to take over the account. The bug was reported and earned a $500 bounty.

lesson.cause: The application kept two separate workflows: one for email management and another for password recovery. When an email was removed, the email‑management code marked it as "Removed" but the password‑reset code never checked that status. Consequently the reset service still considered the old address a valid recovery destination. The flaw stems from not synchronising the user’s current email list with the list used to generate reset tokens. This inconsistency let an attacker trigger a reset for the current email while the link was sent to the previously removed address.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Create a new account using attacker@example.com.
   (No code needed – just fill the registration form.)
   Why: This gives us control of an email that we can later use to receive reset links.

Step 2: Add a second email secondary@example.com and verify it.
   (Again, use the UI to add and confirm the secondary address.)
   Why: The app now stores two emails for the same account.

Step 3: Change the primary email to secondary@example.com.
   (Select secondary@example.com as the primary in the account settings.)
   Why: The account now treats secondary@example.com as the current login email.

Step 4: Remove attacker@example.com from the account.
   (Click the delete/remove button for the old email.)
   Why: The old address is marked as removed, but the app does not purge it from recovery logic.

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Open the Forgot Password page.
   (Navigate to the password‑reset endpoint, usually /forgot-password.)
   Why: This initiates the password‑reset workflow.

Step 6: Submit secondary@example.com as the email to reset.
   
   Why: The system looks up the account by the current email and generates a reset token.

Step 7: Observe that the reset link is sent to attacker@example.com (the removed address).
   
   Why: The reset service still uses the old email list, so the token is mailed to the deleted address.

Step 8: Open the reset link from attacker@example.com and set a new password.
   
   Why: The token is valid, allowing the attacker to change the password and take over the account.

IMPACT
Step 9: Log in with the new password using secondary@example.com.
   
   Why: The attacker now has full access, confirming an account takeover.
lesson.example:
**Fictional target:** https://target.example
**Vulnerable flow:**
1. Register user with primary email user1@target.example.
2. Add secondary email user2@target.example and verify it.
3. Change primary to user2@target.example.
4. Delete user1@target.example.
5. Use the Forgot Password form and enter user2@target.example.
6. The system sends the reset link to user1@target.example (the deleted address).
7. Clicking the link lets the attacker set a new password and log in as the user.
**Why it works:** The password‑reset service does not re‑query the current email list; it uses a stale record that still contains the deleted address, so the reset token is delivered to an email the attacker still controls.
lesson.takeaway: When testing account‑management features, always verify that removing or changing an authentication factor (like an email) is reflected in every related workflow, especially password recovery. Look for inconsistencies between user profile updates and recovery endpoints; tools like Burp Suite can help capture where reset emails are sent. Similar bugs appear in phone‑number removal, security‑question changes, or OAuth redirect updates. A common mistake is assuming that a UI‑level delete automatically revokes backend privileges – always confirm with actual requests and email logs.
lesson.fix:
Update the password‑reset implementation to first fetch the current list of verified emails for the account and ensure the reset token is only sent to addresses that are still marked as active. Pseudo‑code:
```python
active_emails = db.query(UserEmails).filter(user_id=uid, status='verified')
if request.email not in active_emails:
    return error('Email not associated')
# generate token
send_reset(email=request.email, token)
```
Additionally, when an email is removed, invalidate any pending reset tokens that reference it and add regression tests that simulate the add‑verify‑primary‑remove‑reset sequence to catch regressions.

title: I Verified One Email and Claimed Another’s Invitation
summary_en: A business logic flaw in the invitation flow allowed an attacker to claim an invitation sent to one email address using a completely different, uninvited email address. This resulted in an identity mismatch where the attacker gained access to a community role intended for someone else.

lesson.cause: The application failed to enforce a strict link between the invitation token and the specific email address it was issued to. While the invitation was sent to Email A, the registration form allowed the user to edit the email field to Email B. The server-side logic then processed the registration for Email B but associated it with the permissions and metadata (like the displayed profile email) of the original invitation for Email A.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified a member management feature where a 'circle' (a community group) owner can invite new members.
2. The researcher sent an invitation to a test email address: scriptjacker+pentester@gmail.com.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher received an invitation email containing an 'Accept invitation' button.
4. The button linked to a specific URL containing an invitation ID and a secret token (a unique string of characters used as a temporary key).
https://REDACTED/circles/{circle_slug}/membership-invitations/{id}?token={token}
Why: This URL identifies which specific invitation is being accepted. (URL: A web address used to locate a resource).
5. Upon clicking the link, the application redirected to an authentication service ( a separate system that handles logins).
6. The researcher noticed the email field was pre-filled with the invited email but remained editable.

EXPLOITATION
7. The researcher manually changed the email in the browser field from the invited address to a different one: scriptjacker+anotheremail@gmail.com.
8. The researcher clicked 'Continue' to proceed with the registration using the new email.
9. The system sent a verification code (a short numeric password) to the new, uninvited email address.
10. The researcher entered the code and set a password for the new account.
11. The application completed the onboarding process (the initial setup for a new user) without checking if the new email matched the invited one.

IMPACT
12. The researcher checked the circle's member list and saw the new member was added with the 'Contributor' role.
13. Crucially, the member list still displayed the original invited email (Email A), even though the researcher used Email B to sign in.
14. The researcher attempted to log in with Email A and failed, proving the account was not actually tied to that address.
15. The researcher logged in with Email B and successfully accessed the circle and the profile, which still incorrectly displayed Email A's address.
Why: The application logic correctly verified the second email but incorrectly linked that verified identity to the invitation intended for the first email.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'target.example' that lets managers invite employees to a private project. The manager invites 'boss@target.example'. The attacker receives the link (perhaps via a leaked Slack message) and clicks it. The site shows a form: 'Register for Boss's Invite'. The attacker changes the email field from 'boss@target.example' to 'attacker@gmail.com' and submits. The site sends a code to 'attacker@gmail.com'. The attacker enters it and is now logged into the project with 'Boss' permissions, even though the project settings still say 'boss@target.example' is the member. This happens because the server only checks if the token is valid, not if the person using the token is the person the token was made for.
lesson.takeaway: Always test 'pre-filled' forms in invitation or password reset flows. If an application fills in a piece of data for you (like an email or username), try to change it before submitting the request. This is a classic 'Business Logic' flaw where the developer assumes the user will follow the intended path. Look for 'IDOR-adjacent' behavior where a token for Resource A (the invite) is used to create Resource B (the user account) without a cross-check. A common mistake is trusting the client-side input (the email field) over the server-side record associated with the token.

title: $1600 Bounty on a Main Domain
summary_en: Four bugs on a VDP main domain: an open redirect via CRLF injection, a 2FA bypass that accepts email OTPs for phone verification, sensitive account data leaked in the login response before 2FA completes, and a session fixation flaw letting a captured _sc_session cookie skip 2FA on other accounts — $1600 total.
summary_ar: باحث في برنامج VDP خاص اكتشف 4 ثغرات في الدومين الرئيسي: Open Redirect عبر CRLF injection، وثغرة بتسمح باستخدام كود تأكيد الإيميل للتحقق من رقم الهاتف (2FA bypass)، وتسريب بيانات الحساب في الـ login response قبل إتمام الـ 2FA، وSession Fixation بتمكّن من إعادة استخدام كوكي _sc_session لتجاوز الـ 2FA على حسابات تانية — بمجموع جوائز $1600.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause الأساسي إن التطبيق بيفصلش بين قنوات التحقق: نفس الـ API (verify_two_factor_auth) بيستقبل كود الـ OTP سواء جاي من الإيميل أو من الهاتف من غير ما يربط الكود بالقناة اللي اتبعت عليها، فكود الإيميل بيشتغل لتأكيد رقم الهاتف. كمان كوكي _sc_session اللي بتتضبط بعد إتمام الـ 2FA مش مربوطة بالحساب نفسه، فأي حد معاه الكوكي يقدر يستخدمها على حساب تاني من غير 2FA. وفي تسجيل الدخول، الـ response بيرجع بيانات حساسة كاملة (اسم، username، secret token، PIN، عنوان) قبل ما الـ 2FA يخلص أصلاً. والـ redirectTo بيتحقق منه بشكل ناقص سمح بـ CRLF injection عبر /%0d/.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث debu8er كان بيشتغل على برنامج VDP خاص بيهدف إنه يـ triage 20 bug، واتعلم من فيديوهات zseano على يوتيوب. بعد ما اتعملت له دعوة خاصة لبرنامج scope بتاعه wildcard (_.redacted.com)، قرر يركّز على الدومين الرئيسي بس من غير subdomain discovery، وفضل يختبر function ورا function لـ 3 أسابيع من غير أي نتيجة. أول حاجة لفتت نظره إن بعد الـ logout المستخدم بيتحوّل لـ /login?redirectTo=/account، فلما جرّب يغيّر القيمة لـ https://evil.com و //evil.com ما اشتغلش، لكن لما جرّب /%0d/evil.com اتعمل redirect لـ evil.com — بس اتشال كـ duplicate لأن حد تاني بلغها قبله بيوم. بعدها لاحظ إن التطبيق بيستخدم نفس الـ API للتحقق من كود الإيميل وكود الهاتف: POST /api/v1/users/two_factor_auth?email=... للتحقق بالإيميل و POST /api/v1/users/two_factor_auth?phone=... للهاتف، والتحقق النهائي بيحصل عبر POST /api/v1/users/verify_two_factor_auth بجسم JSON زي {"otp_attempt":"116293"}. فافترض إنه يقدر يبدأ phone verification وبعدين يرسل كود الإيميل الجديد مكان كود الهاتف — وطلعت الفرضية صح، فاتقبل النظام كود الإيميل لتأكيد رقم الهاتف، واتصنّفت Medium (6.1) بـ $300. وفي subdomain تابع للدومين الرئيسي (few.redacted.com)، لاحظ إن الـ login response قبل ما يدخل كود الـ 2FA بيرجع بيانات الحساب كاملة: الاسم، اللقب، username، secret token، رقم الهاتف، PIN، والعنوان — من غير ما يكمّل الـ 2FA، واتصنّفت Medium (4.4) بـ $300. آخر حاجة كانت Session Fixation: بعد إتمام الـ 2FA بيتبعت كوكي _sc_session، واكتشف إن الكوكي دي بتتشاف على حسابات تانية، فسجّل الدخول بحساب A وكمّل الـ 2FA والتقط الكوكي، وبعدين استخدمها على حساب B من غير 2FA — اتشالت duplicate على الويب، لكن لما دوّر في تطبيق Android لقى نفس الثغرة في API تاني، واتصنّفت High (7.7) بـ $1000.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أي flow فيه 2FA يستاهل تختبره من زاوية "هل الكود مربوط بالقناة اللي اتبعت عليها؟" — جرّب تبدأ تحقق بالإيميل وبعدين تقدم كود من قناة تانية، ولاحظ لو الـ verify endpoint واحد لكل القنوات. كمان أي كوكي بتتضبط بعد خطوة حساسة (زي الـ 2FA) لازم تتأكد إنها مربوطة بالحساب: اعمل account A و account B واعبر الكوكي بينهم. ولاحظ دايماً الـ response بتاع الـ login قبل إتمام الـ 2FA — لو فيه بيانات حساسة بتتسرب، دي ثغرة مستقلة. ولو لقيت duplicate على الويب، دوّر على نفس الـ endpoint في تطبيقات الموبايل أو APIs تانية — غالباً نفس الـ bug بيتكرر في مكان تاني.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح إن كود الـ OTP يتبقى مربوط بالقناة اللي اتبعت عليها (email أو phone) وبالجلسة اللي بدأت الطلب، والـ verify endpoint لازم يتحقق إن الكود اتبعت للقناة المطلوبة فعلاً مش أي كود صالح. وكوكي _sc_session لازم تكون مربوطة بالحساب والجلسة، وتتبطل (invalidate) لو اتعاد استخدامها أو اتحاول على حساب تاني. والـ login response لازم يرجّع البيانات الحساسة بس بعد إتمام كل خطوات المصادقة، ومتنساش إن الـ redirectTo لازم يتحقق منه بـ allowlist للدومينات الداخلية مع رفض أي CRLF أو protocol-relative URLs زي //evil.com.

title: 2FA Bypass - IDN Mischief
summary_en: A 2FA bypass where an attacker registers a look-alike IDN email (emailOne@gmáil.com) and uses its TOTP code to log into the victim's account (emailOne@gmail.com) — the app normalizes both emails to the same string, so both accounts share the same 2FA seed.
summary_ar: ثغرة في تجاوز الـ 2FA: الباحث سجّل حسابًا بإيميل شبيه (emailOne@gmáil.com) واستخدم كود الـ TOTP الخاص به لتسجيل الدخول في حساب الضحية (emailOne@gmail.com) — لأن النظام يوحّد (normalize) الإيميلين في نص واحد فيتشارك الحسابان نفس الـ 2FA seed.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause هو إن النظام بيعمل normalization للإيميل أثناء عملية الـ 2FA validation، بحيث بيحوّل الأحرف اللي شبه بعضها من أنظمة كتابة مختلفة (زي á و a) إلى أقرب ما يعادلها في ASCII. النتيجة إن emailOne@gmáil.com و emailOne@gmail.com اتعاملوا معاهم كأنهم نفس النص، وبما إن الـ 2FA secret key بيتم استرجاعه بناءً على الإيميل المُوحَّد، الحسابين اتنطبق عليهم نفس الـ seed. الافتراض الخاطئ هنا إن الإيميل معرّف فريد كفاية وإن الـ normalization آمنة في كل مراحل المعالجة — لكن التطبيع ده كسر التفرقة بين حسابين مختلفين فعليًا، فبقى كود 2FA لأي حساب فيهم صالح للتاني.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث كان بيفحص آلية الـ 2FA في الموقع، وبدأ يلعب بفكرة إن الإيميل ممكن يكون معرّف غير موثوق لو النظام بيعمل عليه normalization. أول خطوة سجّل حسابين: الأول بإيميل عادي emailOne@gmail.com، والتاني بإيميل شبهه بالظبط لكن فيه حرف IDN بديل emailOne@gmáil.com (بحرف á بدل a). فعّل الـ 2FA على الحسابين الاتنين، فكل حساب استلم secret key خاص بيه في الـ authenticator app. بعدين من متصفح تاني سجّل دخول على الحساب العادي emailOne@gmail.com بالباسورد، ووصل لشاشة إدخال كود الـ 2FA. بدل ما يستخدم كود الحساب العادي، فتح الـ authenticator app واخد كود الحساب الشبيه emailOne@gmáil.com وكتبه. الموقع قبله وسجّله دخول ناجح — يعني الـ 2FA اتقفزت بالكامل. جرّب العكس كمان: سجّل دخول على الحساب الشبيه واستخدم كود الحساب العادي، ولقى إنه بيشتغل برضه، فالثغرة شغالة في الاتجاهين. من منظور المهاجم، الطريقة العملية هي إنه يعمل حساب شبيه بنفسه ويستخدم كوده لتجاوز حماية حساب الضحية. السبب إن النظام بيوحّد الإيميلين في نص واحد وقت الـ 2FA validation، فيسترجي نفس الـ secret key للحسابين، وبالتالي كودات الـ TOTP بتتبادل بينهم.
lesson.takeaway_ar: لما تلاقي أي تطبيق بيستخدم الإيميل أو الـ username كمفتاح لاسترجاع أسرار أو بيانات (زي 2FA seed، reset tokens، مفاتيح API)، جرّب إنك تسجّل حسابين بإيميلات IDN متشابهة زي gmáil.com و gmail.com ولاحظ لو بيتم معاملتهم كأنهم نفس الحساب. العلامة الأساسية هي وجود أي normalization أو canonicalization للإيميل في أي مرحلة من مراحل الـ flow — حتى لو التسجيل نفسه خزّنهم كحسابين منفصلين. كمان جرّب الـ Unicode homoglyphs في الـ usernames والـ domains بشكل عام، مش بس في الـ 2FA، لأن نفس المشكلة بتظهر في استرجاع كلمة السر، الـ session، أو الـ authorization. لو لقيت إن كود 2FA أو أي secret بيتقبل من حساب تاني، يبقى عندك auth bypass حقيقي يستاهل تقرير.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح إنك متعملش normalization للإيميل أثناء الـ 2FA validation — استخدم الإيميل زي ما هو بالظبط. والأهم إن الـ 2FA secret key يتبقى ويسترجى بمعرّف مستخدم فريد (user ID) مش بالإيميل، زي ما المقال بيوضح في الكود المحسّن: setup_2fa(user_id) بيولّد الـ seed بناءً على الـ user_id، وvalidate_2fa_code(user_id, input_code) بيجيب الـ secret key بالـ user_id. كده حتى لو في إيميلين متشابهين، كل واحد ليه seed مختلف وبتاعه. على مستوى أوسع، أي عملية بتعتمد على الإيميل كمفتاح لازم تتعامل مع الـ Unicode بعناية: إما ترفض الـ homoglyphs وقت التسجيل، أو تخزّن الإيميل بصيغته الأصلية وتستخدم معرّف داخلي منفصل لكل الحسابات.

title: Account takeover on 8 years old public program
summary_en: A race condition in the email-verification flow plus Unicode normalization let an attacker take over any developer account on an 8-year-old public program: they verified an email containing a form-feed character (%0f) that the system treated as identical to the victim's address, then signed in as the victim.
summary_ar: ثغرة race condition في تدفّق التحقق من البريد الإلكتروني مع مشكلة تطبيع Unicode خلّت الباحث يقدر ياخد تحكم كامل في أي حساب developer على برنامج عام عمره 8 سنين: اتأكد من إيميل فيه حرف تحكم %0f النظام عامله زي إيميل الضحية بالظبط، وبعدين سجّل الدخول بحساب الضحية.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause الحقيقي إن نظام التحقق من الإيميل في developer.example.com بيثق في إن إيميل الحساب الأساسي متأكد منه، لكن عملية التحقق مربوطة بنص الإيميل وقت الطلب مش بمعرّف الحساب نفسه. أول ثغرة كانت race condition: الباحث غيّر الإيميل وبعت طلب التحقق في نفس اللحظة بالتوازي، فالنظام أكّد إيميل جديد عمره ما عدّى فحص التحقق الحقيقي. تاني مشكلة إن النظام قبل إيميل فيه حرف تحكم زي %0f (form feed) وخزّنه كحساب مختلف عن victim@gmail.com، لكن في مرحلة تسجيل الدخول على developer.example.com طابقه مع إيميل الضحية كأنهم نفس الحساب. الافتراض الغلط إن تطبيع الإيميل بيحصل بشكل متسق في كل مراحل التطبيق، وده فتح الباب لـ account takeover كامل.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث كان بيفحص برنامج عام قديم عمره 8 سنين فيه موقع أساسي www.example.com وموقع تاني للمطورين developer.example.com، والدخول على موقع المطورين بيتم باختيار حسابك من الموقع الأساسي وبعدها لازم تتأكد من إيميلك. أول حاجة جربها إنه يبايپاس خطوة التحقق دي: عمل حساب بإيميل just@gmail.com، ودخل على developer.example.com وضغط send verification email، وفتح رابط التحقق وهو ماسك الترافيك في Burp، وحوّل طلب التحقق لـ Repeater وDrop الطلب الأصلي. بعدها راح للموقع الأساسي وغيّر إيميله لـ just1@gmail.com، وحوّل طلب تغيير الإيميل كمان لـ Repeater وDrop. عمل group في Repeater وحط الطلبين جنب بعض وبعتهم في نفس اللحظة بالتوازي (parallel)، فالنظام خلّص الحساب بإيميل just1@gmail.com متأكد منه من غير ما الإيميل ده يعدّي أي فحص حقيقي. بلّغ الثغرة دي واتقبلت كـ P4 بمكافأة $200. بعدها فكّر: لو نقدر نعمل حساب developer بإيميل الضحية، نقدر نتأكد منه بنفس الاستغلال السابق وده معناه account takeover. جرّب يغيّر إيميله على الموقع الأساسي لـ victim@gmail.com فجاله error 'something went wrong'. فبدأ يـ fuzz الإيميل بحروف Unicode باستخدام أداة recollapse، ولقى إن الإيميل victim@gmail.com%0f اتقبل. كده عنده حساب بإيميل victim@gmail.com%0f وحساب الضحية victim@gmail.com، وهم حسابين مختلفين تمامًا ومحدش يقدر يوصل لحساب التاني. سجّل دخوله على developer.example.com بإيميل victim@gmail.com%0f، ظهرله email verification prompt، اتأكد من الإيميل بنفس استغلال الـ race condition السابق، وBoom! دخل على حساب الضحية في developer.example.com — account takeover كامل.
lesson.takeaway_ar: الدرس هنا إن أي flow فيه تحقق من الإيميل أو تغيير إيميل لازم تختبره كـ race condition: لو في طلبين (تغيير إيميل + تأكيد) ممكن يتسلسلوا بالتوازي، جرّبهم في Burp Repeater group. كمان أي حقل إيميل بيقبل إدخال فيه حروف تحكم أو Unicode غريبة هو إشارة قوية لمشكلة تطبيع — جرّب fuzzing بحروف زي %0f و%0a و%09 وعلامات التشكيل. العلامة اللي تدلّك إن الفئة دي موجودة: رسالة خطأ عامة زي 'something went wrong' مع الإيميل النضيف، ونجاح مع نسخة فيها حرف مخفي. أدوات زي recollapse بتوفّر عليك وقت كبير في توليد الـ payloads دي.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح يبدأ من إن التحقق من الإيميل لازم يكون مربوط بمعرّف الحساب (account ID) مش بنص الإيميل، وأي تغيير للإيميل لازم يلغي أي verification token قديم فورًا. كمان لازم يكون فيه تطبيع موحّد للإيميلات قبل التخزين والمقارنة: شيل حروف التحكم زي %0f، حوّل للحروف الصغيرة، وطبّق punycode على الـ Unicode — بحيث victim@gmail.com%0f يتبقى نفس victim@gmail.com أو يُرفض كإدخال غير صالح. عملية تغيير الإيميل مع التأكيد لازم تتحط في transaction واحدة atomic عشان مفيش حالة وسطية يتسجل فيها إيميل جديد متأكد. وفي النهاية validation على مستوى الإدخال يرفض أي حرف تحكم في حقل الإيميل من الأساس.

title: How I Got $150 on HackerOne for My First Bug
summary_en: A private HackerOne program paid $150 for a 2FA recovery-code hygiene flaw: old recovery codes stayed valid after 2FA was disabled and re-enabled, letting attackers bypass 2FA and take over accounts.
summary_ar: برنامج خاص على HackerOne دفع $150 مقابل ثغرة في إدارة recovery codes الخاصة بـ 2FA: الكودات القديمة فضلت صالحة بعد تعطيل وإعادة تفعيل 2FA، مما سمح للمهاجم بعمل bypass لـ 2FA والاستيلاء على الحسابات.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause هنا إن النظام مش بيعمل revoke للـ recovery codes القديمة لما المستخدم يعطّل 2FA. الافتراض الخاطئ في التصميم كان إن إعادة تفعيل 2FA هتولّد كودات جديدة وبالتالي الكودات القديمة هتبوظ تلقائيًا — لكن السيرفر فضل بيقبل الكودات اللي اتولّدت قبل إعادة التفعيل. المشكلة مش في خوارزمية التوليد نفسها، لكن في إدارة دورة حياة الأسرار (secret lifecycle): مفيش أي آلية لإبطال الكودات الصادرة سابقًا عند تغيير حالة 2FA. فبالتالي أي recovery code تسرّب أو اتسرق قبل كده يفضل صالح للأبد حتى بعد ما المستخدم يعمل disable وإعادة enable.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: في يونيو 2024 كان الباحث بيختبر تدفق الـ 2FA في برنامج خاص على HackerOne، وقرر يفحص دورة حياة الـ recovery codes كاملة بدل ما يكتفي باختبار تسجيل الدخول العادي. الخطوة الأولى كانت إنه فعّل 2FA على حسابه وولّد recovery codes وحفظها في مكان آمن. بعدها عطّل 2FA من إعدادات الحساب، وبعدين أعاد تفعيله تاني من نفس الإعدادات. هنا لاحظ إن النظام ما عملهوش أي إشارة إن الكودات القديمة اتبطلت — فقرر يختبر الفرضية دي عمليًا. سجّل خروجه من الحساب، وبعدين حاول يسجل دخول تاني مستخدمًا واحد من الـ recovery codes القديمة اللي اتولّدت قبل إعادة التفعيل. النتيجة كانت إن الكود القديم اشتغل وخلّاه يدخل الحساب من غير ما يطلب منه كود 2FA جديد. يعني رغم إن 2FA اتقفل واتفتح تاني، النظام فضل قايل إن الكودات القديمة لسه صالحة. الباحث وثّق الخطوات دي بالظبط — Enable 2FA، Save Codes، Disable 2FA، Re-enable 2FA، Sign Out، وبعدين Login Attempt بالكود القديم — ورفع تقرير مفصل على HackerOne فيه وصف المشكلة وخطوات إعادة الإنتاج والأثر المتوقع. الفريق الأمني أكد الثغرة ودفعله $150. الثغرة دي اتسمّت في التقرير Incorrect 2FA Recovery Code Hygiene، وبتسمح لأي حد معاه كود قديم إنه يعمل bypass للـ 2FA ويدخل حساب المستخدم.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أي تطبيق فيه 2FA لازم تختبر دورة حياته كاملة مش بس تسجيل الدخول: فعّل، عطّل، أعد التفعيل، وبعدين جرّب الكودات القديمة والـ TOTP secret القديم. العلامة اللي بتدل على الفئة دي إن النظام لما يعيد تفعيل 2FA ما بيظهرش أي تغيير في صلاحية الكودات القديمة أو ما بيطلبش إعادة تحقق. نفس النمط بيظهر كمان في تغيير الباسورد أو الإيميل أو الـ API keys — دايماً اسأل نفسك: هل الأسرار القديمة اتبطلت فعلًا على السيرفر ولا لسه شغالة؟ ولو لقيت إن حالة أمنية بتتغير من غير ما الأسرار القديمة تتبطل، يبقى قدامك ثغرة تستاهل تقرير.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح إن السيرفر يعمل invalidation صريحة لكل الـ recovery codes وكل أسرار الـ TOTP القديمة لحظة ما المستخدم يعطّل 2FA، ويفضل يرفضها حتى لو أعاد التفعيل بعدين. عند إعادة التفعيل لازم يتولّد secret جديد وكودات جديدة تمامًا، وأي كود قديم يترفض بـ error واضح. كمان الـ recovery codes المفروض تكون single-use — أي كود بيتستخدم مرة واحدة وبعدها يتبطل فورًا حتى لو كان صحيح. ويفضل تسجيل كل عملية enable/disable في audit log عشان تقدر تتبع أي كود اتولّد وإمتى اتبطل.

title: Exploring Anti-Phishing Measures in Microsoft 365 – Certitude Blog
summary_en: Certitude showed that Microsoft 365's First Contact Safety Tip can be hidden with CSS (white-on-white text) and Outlook's signed/encrypted badges can be spoofed, stripping anti-phishing warnings from emails. Microsoft confirmed the finding via MSRC but declined to fix it, calling it below the servicing bar.
summary_ar: أثبت باحثو Certitude أن تنبيه First Contact Safety Tip في Microsoft 365 يمكن إخفاؤه عبر CSS (نص أبيض على خلفية بيضاء)، وأن شارات التوقيع/التشفير في Outlook يمكن تزويرها، ما يزيل تحذيرات مكافحة التصيّد من الرسائل. أكدت Microsoft صحة الاكتشاف عبر MSRC لكنها رفضت إصلاحه باعتباره دون مستوى المعالجة الفورية.

lesson.cause_ar: السبب الجذري إن First Contact Safety Tip بيتم إلحاقه (prepend) بجسم الإيميل HTML نفسه، يعني التنبيه الأمني بيعيش جوه محتوى يتحكم فيه المهاجم بالكامل. الافتراض الخاطئ في التصميم إن التنبيه اللي بيضيفه السيرفر محمي من العبث، لكن الحقيقة إنه بيترسم من نفس الـ markup اللي بيوصله من المرسل. محرك العرض في Outlook بيمنع قواعد الإخفاء الشائعة زي display:none و opacity:0 بسبب الـ inline CSS والقيود، لكنه مش بيمنع تغيير الألوان، فتحويل النص والخلفية للأبيض بيخلي التنبيه غير مرئي. كمان Outlook بيحوّل أي عنوان إيميل مكتوب بنقطة عادية لرابط mailto تلقائيًا، فاستخدم الباحث Unicode U+2024 بدل النقطة عشان التزوير يفضل متطابق. النتيجة: تحذير أمني موجود في الصفحة لكنه غير مرئي، وشارات التوقيع/التشفير قابلة للتزوير، فبينهار الغرض الكامل من الإجراء.
lesson.walkthrough_ar:
الخطوة 1: السياق — الباحث كان بيفحص إجراءات مكافحة التصيّد في Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online Protection و Defender)، وتحديدًا First Contact Safety Tip اللي بيظهر لما تستلم إيميل من عنوان مش بتتعامل معه عادة، برسالة نصها "You don't often get email from xyz@example.com".
الخطوة 2: الملاحظة الأولى — التنبيه بيتضاف (prepend) لجسم الإيميل HTML نفسه، يعني بيبقى جوه محتوى يتحكم فيه المهاجم، وبالتالي ممكن يتعدل عرضه عبر وسوم CSS style.
الخطوة 3: التجربة الأولى — حاول يخفي الجدول اللي فيه التنبيه بقواعد CSS شائعة: display: none و height: 0px و opacity: 0.
الخطوة 4: النتيجة — القواعد دي مش شغالة، إما بسبب الـ inline CSS الموجود في العناصر نفسها أو بسبب عدم دعم محرك العرض اللي Outlook بيستخدمه.
الخطوة 5: الحل — بدل الإخفاء الكامل، غيّر الألوان: خلفية بيضاء ونص أبيض مع font-size: 0px، فالتنبيه بيترسم لكنه مش بيبان.
الخطوة 6: الكود المستخدم:
<head><style> a { display: none; } td div { color: white; font-size: 0px; } table tbody tr td { background-color: white !important; color: white !important; } </style></head>
الخطوة 7: ليه شغالة — التنبيه لسه موجود في الـ DOM لكن ألوانه بقت مطابقة للخلفية البيضاء، فالعين مش بتلتقطه، و!important بتتغلب على أي أنماط تانية.
الخطوة 8: إثبات الأثر — الصورة بتوضح إن التنبيه مش ظاهر في جسم الإيميل نهائيًا، لكن الـ preview (المظلل بالأحمر) لسه بيبدأ بنص التنبيه.
الخطوة 9: خطوة إضافية — تزوير شارات التوقيع/التشفير اللي Outlook بيضيفها للإيميلات الموقّعة، عبر جدول فيه نص "Signed By nimmerrichtermarc@gmail.com" وصورتين base64 كشارات.
